Good morning. 1 I would like to thank our hosts, the Banco Central do Brasil, the Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas (ASBA), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), and the Financial Stability Institute, for bringing us together. Banking supervisors around the world are tasked with ensuring the safety and soundness of the banking system. To be effective in this work, bank supervisory and regulatory frameworks must be forward looking to anticipate future risks. Today, I will discuss three ways in which modernizing our supervision and regulatory frameworks can enhance our ability to be effective. First, we must learn the appropriate lessons from failures of supervisory effectiveness. Recent experience in the United States demonstrates that it is not sufficient to identify financial risks. Supervisors must also have the authority, accountability, and judgment to act before those risks are realized. Second, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must be regularly revisited to keep pace with the evolving financial landscape. These frameworks must focus on the most material risks, enable timely decisions, and adapt to rapidly changing financial markets and technologies. This is a priority both for the Federal Reserve and our international colleagues, including those on the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the BCBS. Third, banking supervisors throughout the Americas must be effective. Our shared history, deeply interconnected economies, and regional financial challenges support alignment of our interests in maintaining strong institutions for supervisory cooperation. ASBA can play a role in that effort. These points are closely related. Effective supervision requires sound judgment. Sound judgment must be supported by modern frameworks. And cooperation among supervisors in the Americas supports strengthening both. Learning from Banking Failures: Information Must Lead to Action One of the most valuable responsibilities of any supervisory authority is to learn the right lessons from failure and adjust accordingly. The March 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), and subsequent discussions about what went wrong and paths for reform, provide a useful case study. Extraordinary measures were taken to address banking system stress in the wake of SVB's failure, and fundamental questions remain regarding the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve System's supervisory function. Earlier reviews of the bank's failure provided important information but did not consider questions about shortcomings in the Federal Reserve's supervisory approach or identify opportunities to address long-standing weaknesses in our supervision. When I became Vice Chair for Supervision, I initiated an independent review of SVB's failure. The initial findings of that review released in September were sobering. The review validated that supervisors identified the bank's fundamental vulnerabilities well before its failure. 2 Those vulnerabilities included substantial interest rate risk, a highly concentrated and predominantly uninsured deposit base, and inadequate preparedness to meet liquidity demands. These were not unfamiliar or complicated risks to understand. They have been common risks throughout history, were present at the time of SVB's failure, and continue to be fundamental banking risks today. Yet our supervisory process failed to produce timely and effective action to address them. A central lesson is that the failure of supervision was not a failure to obtain information. It was a failure to translate information into timely, decisive action. The review identified a long-standing supervisory problem of consultation without conclusion or action, uncertainty about decisionmaking authority, and a lack of accountability. Supervisors identified concerns, documented weaknesses, and discussed vulnerabilities. But the process did not result in prompt action to require the bank to address material risks that ultimately led to its failure. One particularly revealing finding illustrates the problem. Between 2019 and March 2023, supervisors cited 54 supervisory matters that required attention. Yet no finding required SVB to shorten the maturity profile of its securities portfolio or restructure the held-to-maturity book, which were material financial risks that contributed to the bank's failure. Instead, many supervisory findings focused on process concerns. While interest rate risk was discussed, the approach criticized how the bank measured the risk but did not direct the bank to reduce it. Supervisors engaged in extensive supervisory activity, produced considerable documentation, and created a substantial record of identified concerns. But the risks that were most material—the risks that affected the bank's financial condition—were not addressed. This experience should encourage every supervisory authority to consider how it measures its own effectiveness. We should not measure success by the number of examinations conducted, findings issued, and reports produced. Instead, we must measure success by whether our work results in the timely identification, mitigation, and remediation of material risks. A supervisory organization can be extraordinarily busy without being effective. Excessive process can become a major obstacle to effective supervision. When responsibility is unclear, when decisionmaking authority is fragmented, or when supervisors believe that every judgment must be supported by perfect information, the supervisory process can delay action until it is too late. The independent review showed that these organizational and cultural weaknesses can have serious consequences. Supervisory decisions must be grounded in sound analysis, appropriate legal authority, and professional judgment. But those decisions must also be timely. A supervisory judgment that arrives after the opportunity for effective intervention has passed may have little practical value. Our goal must be to reach reasonably informed decisions in time to influence outcomes, rather than achieving perfect certainty after the opportunity to act has passed. This lesson becomes even more important as supervisory authorities adopt new technology. Artificial intelligence (or super intelligence), advanced analytics, and other supervisory technologies have the potential to improve the identification of emerging risks and our understanding of complex financial relationships. This can provide supervisors access to more information more quickly than ever before. But more information is not necessarily better supervision. The SVB experience should remind us that information alone is not a substitute for judgment and timely action. Therefore, our approach must be to modernize supervisory culture while upgrading our supervisory technology. Clear lines of responsibility and decisionmaking authority are imperative. The ultimate measure of successful and effective supervision is the ability to recognize material risks and act effectively while there is still time to influence the outcome. Modernizing Our Supervisory and Regulatory Frameworks Second, we must ensure our regulatory and supervisory frameworks enable the identification of material risks, sound decisionmaking, and supervisory response in a rapidly changing financial system. Our priorities should be to ensure supervisors are trained to identify and focus attention on material risks, enable timely decisionmaking and clear accountability, and establish a regulatory framework that encourages innovation without compromising safety and soundness. The Federal Reserve is pursuing each of these objectives. First, we are modernizing the conduct of supervision. Our Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles refocuses supervision on identifying material risks and taking prompt, proportionate action to address them. The principles emphasize risk-focused supervision, tailored to the size, complexity, and risk profile of individual institutions. They call for clearer expectations, greater transparency, and the exercise of sound professional judgment rather than excessive reliance on procedural requirements, checklists, or documentation. They also seek to align examination findings and supervisory ratings more closely with material risks, reduce unnecessary duplication, and streamline the resolution of supervisory concerns. Our objective is not to produce more supervisory findings or more documentation. It is to ensure that supervision identifies the risks that matter most and results in timely action to address them. 3 Second, we are changing how we organize the supervisory function itself. The independent review highlighted a fundamental organizational weakness, a mismatch between decisionmaking authority and accountability. The Federal Reserve's supervisory responsibilities have historically been carried out through a complex structure involving the Board, the 12 Reserve Banks, and numerous committees. That structure has not always provided accountability, identified clear lines of responsibility, or supported timely decisions. To address these shortcomings, we have begun reorganizing our supervisory function. The reorganization preserves the expertise and relationships of local examination teams while providing clearer lines of accountability through regional leadership. This reorganization is intended to clarify decisionmaking authority, streamline escalation, reduce unnecessary layers of review, and strengthen accountability for supervisory outcomes. We are also examining the role of committees and other internal processes that can cloud responsibility or delay action. When supervisors identify a material risk, there should be no ambiguity about who has the authority to act, who is responsible for ensuring that action is taken, and the importance of elevating decisions for prompt action when necessary. 4 Third, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must keep pace with innovation. Financial markets and technology are evolving rapidly. Artificial intelligence, digital assets, payment technology, and innovative business models create opportunities to improve efficiency, expand financial services, and support economic growth. Our responsibility is to establish clear and predictable rules of the road so that financial institutions can confidently pursue responsible innovation while managing the material risks associated with new activities. This requires a careful balance. Regulatory frameworks that are overly prescriptive or unnecessarily burdensome can discourage innovation, limit competition, and push financial activity outside the regulated banking system. But uncertainty about regulatory expectations can also discourage innovation. Financial institutions need to understand the standards that apply to new activities and the risks they are expected to manage. A modern regulatory framework should provide clarity about objectives and expectations while allowing sufficient flexibility for financial institutions to develop new products, adopt new technology, and respond to changing market conditions. These three elements—risk-focused supervision, clear organizational accountability, and adaptable regulation—are also central to the broader international modernization agenda. As chair of the FSB's Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, I have worked with colleagues from around the world to develop common principles to guide modernization efforts. In October, the FSB released a consultation report proposing eight high-level principles intended to help authorities improve the effectiveness, efficiency, risk focus, coherence, and adaptability of their regulatory and supervisory frameworks. The principles recognize that our frameworks must remain responsive to emerging financial risks and technological developments. They emphasize appropriate tailoring, transparency, and accountability as well as the importance of periodically evaluating whether regulatory requirements remain fit for their intended purposes. As the FSB and the BCBS carry this work forward, they must take care that the assumptions underlying work commissioned in response to bank failures like that of SVB are appropriately validated. Post-failure analyses can embed untested assumptions about what went wrong and what should be done about it, and those assumptions can then be relied upon to shape international standards. Before such conclusions inform global policy, they should be tested against the evidence and confirmed across different jurisdictions and banking models. Importantly, the principles acknowledge that implementation must reflect national legal frameworks and circumstances. 5 That recognition is especially relevant to the Americas, where banking systems differ considerably in their size, structure, complexity, and economic roles. Modernization does not require every jurisdiction to adopt identical institutional arrangements or supervisory practices. It should provide a common set of principles that can be implemented effectively within different financial systems. What matters is that our frameworks produce the outcomes we need: timely identification and mitigation of material risks, clear accountability, predictable regulatory expectations, and the flexibility to respond to change. Strengthening the Supervisory Community in the Americas The third and final topic for my discussion today is the importance of strengthening practical cooperation among the community of supervisors in the Americas. This priority has taken on particular importance in light of recent developments in banking systems throughout the hemisphere. Recent episodes of banking stress serve as a reminder of how quickly financial vulnerabilities can become more serious, and how important the strength and credibility of supervisory institutions can be to maintaining public confidence. They also underscore the broader lesson that effective supervision depends not simply on the existence of rules, but on the ability of institutions and their supervisors to implement those rules, exercise sound judgment, and take action when it is needed. They also provide further support for strengthening the relationships, technical capabilities, and practical cooperation among supervisors across our hemisphere. But there is another reason why cooperation among the countries of the Americas deserves particular attention. The Americas are a community of countries with deep historical, commercial, financial, and institutional connections. Our banking systems are linked through trade finance, investment, cross-border lending, payments, and remittances. Economic developments in one part of the hemisphere can have direct and sometimes immediate consequences for financial institutions and communities elsewhere in the region. These connections support economic growth and financial development. But they also create transmission channels for financial stability risks. We have seen this repeatedly throughout our shared history. The Latin American debt crisis of the 1980s provides one important example. 6 As debt-servicing difficulties spread across Latin America, they posed serious challenges both for the countries directly affected and for international banks with significant exposures throughout the region. The response required extensive cooperation among governments, central banks, commercial banks, and international financial institutions. That cooperation was indispensable. However, the crisis imposed enormous economic costs, and some responses delayed the resolution of underlying vulnerabilities. The experience demonstrated a fundamental reality—that financial stability risks do not respect national boundaries, and effective responses often require close cooperation among authorities across borders. More than four decades later, financial relationships throughout the Americas have become more extensive and complex. But our common interests extend beyond managing financial stability. Our banking systems confront a range of shared challenges, including exposure to cross-border capital flows, commodity cycles, exchange rate movements, and shifts in international financing conditions. Our shared challenges also include the opportunities and risks associated with digital banking, new payments technology, and the growing use of artificial intelligence. There are also challenges that have a particularly significant regional dimension, like remittances and cross-border payments that are critically important to households and businesses throughout the Americas. The efficiency, accessibility, and integrity of these financial channels have important implications for financial inclusion and economic opportunity. At the same time, financial institutions and supervisors must contend with threats arising from money laundering, fraud, illicit financial networks, and transnational criminal organizations. These threats can permeate borders, crossing multiple jurisdictions, and place significant demands on supervisory resources. These threats reinforce the importance of strong supervisory relationships, effective information sharing, and coordination among authorities. International standard-setting bodies such as the Basel Committee, the FSB, and the Financial Stability Institute offer useful reference points and forums for dialogue. Global standards can be a helpful input. But they do not replace the working relationships, regional knowledge, and practical coordination that develop among authorities facing common challenges. They work best when they acknowledge and incorporate national and regional circumstances. This is where I see a valuable role for ASBA. It can provide a forum devoted to the financial systems, supervisory challenges, and institutional relationships of the Americas. Its strength is its regional focus. Bringing together supervisors from across the hemisphere, ASBA can help ensure that our regional priorities receive the attention they deserve, that our supervisory authorities develop the capabilities they need, and that the practical experience of each member country informs the continuing development of international supervisory standards. We should continue building on this important role for ASBA. I see several opportunities to strengthen that role. First, we should deepen the exchange of practical supervisory lessons. The experience of SVB demonstrates why this is important. We should be willing to carefully examine bank failures and supervisory challenges, identify the institutional and operational factors that contributed to them, and determine how those lessons can improve supervisory practice. These exchanges should go beyond identifying vulnerabilities in individual institutions. They should examine how supervisors make decisions, how concerns are escalated, and how institutional arrangements can either facilitate or delay effective action. ASBA can facilitate that exchange through case studies, technical discussions, and practical training. Second, we should strengthen supervisory leadership and institutional capabilities. Technical expertise is essential to effective bank supervision. But the ability to identify risks is only part of the job. Supervisors must also be able to prioritize competing concerns, exercise professional judgment, communicate difficult conclusions, and take timely action. These capabilities can be strengthened through leadership development, secondments, professional exchanges, and realistic supervisory exercises. Strong supervisory institutions also require clear governance arrangements, well-defined responsibilities, and accountability for decisions. Building these capabilities should be an important focus of our regional cooperation. Third, we should cooperate more closely on emerging technologies and new financial activities. Artificial intelligence, digital banking, cybersecurity, and innovative payments technologies present many of the same questions for supervisors throughout the hemisphere. How can these technologies improve risk identification and supervisory efficiency? How should supervisors evaluate the risks associated with new business models? These questions will benefit from practical cooperation. There is significant value in sharing experience with supervisory technologies, analytical methods, and approaches to emerging risks, rather than requiring every authority to develop solutions independently. Fourth, we should continue strengthening cross-border crisis preparedness and supervisory relationships. Relationships established during stable periods can become indispensable as financial conditions deteriorate. When an internationally active bank encounters serious difficulties, timely communication through previously established channels for cooperation can make a meaningful difference. Supervisors should understand the responsibilities of their counterparts, have established mechanisms for exchanging appropriate information, and be prepared to coordinate when circumstances require it. We should continue investing in those relationships now. Finally, I believe the Americas should play an active role in shaping the international modernization agenda. The FSB's proposed principles create an important opportunity for this engagement. ASBA can help bring practical supervisory experience into international discussions, identify implementation challenges, and contribute to improving the effectiveness of international standards. Regional cooperation should not simply be a mechanism for transmitting standards developed elsewhere. It should also help inform the continuing development and practical implementation of those standards. As we pursue regulatory and supervisory modernization, I hope that ASBA will continue to be an active partner in this work. The Federal Reserve values its relationships with supervisory authorities throughout the Americas, and we look forward to strengthening those relationships through ASBA and our other bilateral and multilateral partnerships. Together, our objective should be to strengthen supervisory effectiveness, improve the resilience of our banking systems, and support the financial intermediation that is essential to economic prosperity. In the Americas, we have a special opportunity to do that together by strengthening our supervisory capabilities, deepening our cooperation, and ensuring that ASBA remains responsive to the distinctive needs and priorities of our region. Closing Thoughts The lessons of SVB are clear: identifying risk is not enough. Supervision succeeds only when information leads to timely, decisive action. As we modernize our frameworks, we must focus on material risks, establish clear accountability, and remain adaptable to innovation, while recognizing that each jurisdiction will implement these principles in ways suited to its individual system. I will conclude with a call to use venues like ASBA to share the hard lessons of failure, to build supervisory leadership and capability, to cooperate on emerging technology, and to invest now in the cross-border relationships needed in a crisis. Let us bring these shared experiences into the FSB's modernization work, so that the principles reflect the realities of the Americas. 1. Published on  
        25 November 2026 News release The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) have today published revised rules designed to support securitisation’s contribution to economic growth. Securitisation allows a firm to divide loans into 'tranches' which have different risk profiles. Investors may buy some or all tranches, providing the firm with funding for further lending, while the interest from the loans pays the investors, who also absorb some of the losses when borrowers do not repay their loans. Securitisation can help firms manage their funding and risk, supporting further lending to businesses and households. Today’s changes are designed to make the regulators’ requirements more proportionate and less prescriptive, helping reduce unnecessary costs for firms, while maintaining financial stability. They include: Simplifying due diligence and transparency requirements, holding investors and issuers to the same standards of understanding and disclosing risks without being overly prescriptive; Introducing more flexible risk retention options, while ensuring firms keep at least 5% of a securitisation's value at risk; Allowing some simple and prudent re-securitisations to support firms' funding and liquidity needs, while continuing the ban on the wider practice. The reforms are also estimated to reduce industry costs by around £168 million over the next decade while maintaining important safeguards and high standards. Phil Evans, Director of Prudential Policy at the Prudential Regulation Authority, said: 'Securitisation is an important part of a modern financial system. It is obvious that we must never go back to the dangerous practices in place before the great financial crisis, but we shouldn’t go too far the other way either and stifle lending. Today’s final rules strike that balance and should encourage firms to lend more to households and businesses.' Jon Relleen, Director of Infrastructure and Exchanges at the Financial Conduct Authority, said: 'Strong capital markets are vital to support economic growth. By simplifying the UK's securitisation regime, we’re reducing unnecessary costs, giving firms and investors greater flexibility, and better reflecting market practice. The changes support more effective markets but crucially also maintain high standards to mitigate potential risks.' Notes to editors Read the full policy statement . The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework. This policy statement follows a number of recent PRA and FCA measures aimed at supporting growth, competitiveness and innovation in UK financial services while maintaining financial stability, including, exploring ideas to support the growth of credit unions; simplifying the Senior Managers & Certification regime; and automatically increasing over 100 PRA regulatory thresholds to provide certainty for firms. The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework. The rules are near-final because the related statutory instrument has been laid by HM Treasury but has not yet been made. The FCA intends to make the final rules shortly after the statutory instrument has been made and does not expect any significant changes to them. The PRA has published final rules at the same time. For further details of estimated costs saving, please refer to the cost benefit analyses set out in FCA Consultation Paper CP26/6 . The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. For the first time since comparable data were collected in 2016, [ 1 ] cards were used more often than cash at physical locations, such as shops. In 2026 cards accounted for 45% of transactions, compared with 44% for cash. Mobile payments increased to 9%, from 6% in 2024. While payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences remain stable. When paying in a shop, 54% preferred cards or other cashless methods, 22% preferred cash and 23% had no clear preference. A large majority of respondents attach importance to retaining a choice of payment methods. For 82% of euro area consumers, it is important to have the option to pay digitally, while 62% value the option of paying with cash. Only 3% reported never using cash. “Digital means of payment are becoming more important in day-to-day transactions, but choice is what really matters for Europeans,” said Piero Cipollone, member of the ECB’s Executive Board. “The ECB will continue to ensure citizens have the freedom to choose how to pay, by safeguarding cash while preparing for the possible issuance of its digital equivalent, the digital euro.” Most consumers continue to find it easy to access cash, although the share declined to 85%, from 87% in 2024. Among those who had tried to withdraw cash from an ATM during the previous year, 19% experienced difficulties. In all euro area countries, at least 12% of consumers experienced non-acceptance of mobile or card payments at least once in the month preceding the survey. The survey covered 51,551 respondents across the euro area. Data were collected in two rounds: the first between 29 September and 27 November 2025, and the second between 16 March and 15 May 2026. For media queries, please contact Alessandro Speciale , tel.: +49 172 1670791. Previous editions of the SPACE study were published in 2019, 2022 and 2024. title: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability.
body: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability. Oran Kelly Research Scientist, Google DeepMind Nov 24, 2026 Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the live leaderboard , or read our technical report . To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)

title: Treasury Identifies Nearly $15 Billion in Potential Iranian Shadow Banking
body: November 23, 2026 WASHINGTON —In a new Financial Trend Analysis , the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) identified approximately $14.7 billion of financial activity from January 2025 to August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking. As part of their compliance requirements, U.S. financial institutions flag suspicious activity to FinCEN, making it available to law enforcement and national security agencies. “Financial institutions are often the first line of defense in denying Iranian regime-linked funds access to the U.S. economy,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent . “Treasury will continue to sever the financial lifelines on which the regime relies to fund its military, weapons programs, and terror proxies.” The trends and methods associated with potential Iranian shadow banking remained relatively consistent through 2026. Potential Iranian shadow banking networks continue to be connected across continents, most prominently in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Hong Kong, and Singapore, and by the oil, shipping, investment, technology procurement, and other industries. Key Findings The most common routes for funds flagged by financial institutions were: from mainland China-based banks to UAE-based banks: approximately $2.6 billion; Singapore-based banks to UAE-based banks: approximately $981 million; and United Kingdom-based banks to UAE-based banks: approximately $922 million. The potential exploitation of companies registered in the Marshall Islands and British Virgin Islands, usually at addresses linked to corporate registries, emerged as an area of concern. Potential Iran-linked companies were involved in a diverse array of businesses, including shipping, trading, and oil. Reporting Suspicious Iran-Related Activity To support financial institutions in their Bank Secrecy Act reporting, FinCEN has previously issued several publications that highlight red flags on Iran-linked actors: FinCEN Advisory on the Iranian Regime’s Illicit Oil Smuggling Activities, Shadow Banking Networks, and Weapons Procurement Efforts (June 2025) FinCEN Alert on the Use of Front Companies, Financial Facilitators, and Digital Asset Infrastructure by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to Evade Sanctions and Launder Proceeds (May 2026) FinCEN Alert to Counter Iranian Procurement Efforts for its Commercial Aviation Industry (September 2026) FinCEN Alert to Counter Iranian Abuse of Religious Charity Networks (October 2026) Through its whistleblower incentive program , FinCEN welcomes tips on Iran-related illicit finance . Individuals located in the United States or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations may be eligible for an award if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. As highlighted in FinCEN’s recent Bulletin ( available in several languages ), this includes information about violations of the Bank Secrecy Act or Office of Foreign Assets Control-administered sanctions programs that may involve the use of Iranian proxies and facilitators operating outside of Iran. ###

title: Operation Economic Outcast Disrupts Iran’s Global Shadow Banking Networks
body: November 23, 2026 WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury sanctioned over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel in a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran’s global shadow banking networks. As Iran’s economy remains battered by punishing economic sanctions and its oil revenues continue to decline, the regime’s shadow banking facilitators have increasingly failed to repatriate dwindling export earnings while simultaneously enriching themselves by stealing state resources that rightfully belong to the Iranian people. “Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent . “Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.” Today’s action targets the financial infrastructure that underpins much of Iran’s remaining foreign trade, disrupting the exchange houses, front companies, and facilitators that move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions. This action is being taken pursuant to the following Executive Orders (E.O.): E.O. 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, including Iran’s financial sector; E.O. 13224, as amended, a counter-terrorism designation authority; and E.O. 13871, which targets persons operating in various sectors of Iran’s metals industry. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026, dubbed Economic D-Day, Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime. Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror. Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran.  Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. It also expanded secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . EXCHANGE HOUSES AND RAHBAR COMPANIES Iran’s shadow banking system is overseen by the Central Bank of Iran and relies on dozens of Iran-based exchange houses and “rahbar companies,” bank affiliates that manage sanctions evasion networks for their Iran-based clients. Exchange houses and rahbar companies work hand-in-hand to facilitate the financial underpinnings of Iran’s international trade through thousands of front companies in multiple jurisdictions, most prominently, but not exclusively, in Dubai and Hong Kong. Billions of dollars move through the international financial system in this fashion, sustaining the last remnants of Iran’s foreign trade. Iran-based Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company (Nesim Baharan) operates as the rahbar company for Bank Sarmayeh and works closely with Iranian exchange houses and their front companies to facilitate transactions on behalf of Bank Sarmayeh’s Iranian clients, which include major Iranian petrochemical companies. Sayyed Mohammad Jalali , Valiollah Hemmati , and Ali Kalhor act as senior officials of Nesim Baharan. Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Sayyed Mohammad Jalali, Valiollah Hemmati, and Ali Kalhor are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company. Iran-based Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company (Fashki Exchange) and Mellat Exchange Company are exchange houses operating within Iran’s shadow banking system. Mina Fashki and Farzad Fashki own and operate Fashki Exchange, while Mahmoud Akhlaghi , Parviz Fazlju , and Mohammad Hossein Abbasi are officials of Mellat Exchange Company. Note : This graphic updates an April 2026 version to include Bank Sarmayeh and its rahbar. Fashki Exchange and Mellat Exchange Company are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Mina Fashki and Farzad Fashki are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Fashki Exchange. Mahmoud Akhlaghi, Parviz Fazlju, and Mohammad Hossein Abbasi are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Mellat Exchange Company. Dubai-based Grand Target Heavy Equipment and Machinery Spare Parts Trading L.L.C , Recaz Star General Trading LLC , Meethale Raw Materials Trading Company LLC , Hemraj Trading L.L.C , Ewan Al Madeena General Trading LLC , OGA Global General Trading L.L.C , Dexterous Global DMCC , Khore Al Hilal Goods Wholesalers Trading LLC , Türkiye-based Bogazici Gumrukleme Ithalat Ihracat Turizm Petrol Urunleri Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi , and Hong Kong-based Grandez Trading Limited are exchange house front companies used by Iran’s rahbar network to facilitate thousands of cross-border payments, worth billions of dollars, on behalf of Iranian clients. These front companies have enabled Iran to carry out thousands of financial transactions through the rahbar network. Khore Al Hilal Goods Wholesalers Trading LLC has been used extensively by U.S.-sanctioned Iranian exchange houses Opal Exchange, also known as Pedram Pirouzan Exchange , and Omid Sepah Exchange to move millions of dollars for Iranian Bank Sepah. Grandez Trading Limited is a front company used by the U.S.-sanctioned Iranian exchange house Mohsen Khandan and Partners Exchange . Recaz Star General Trading LLC has sent and received hundreds of payments totaling over $170 million from persons associated with Sadaf Exchange . OGA Global General Trading LLC has overseen millions of dollars’ worth of payments for the National Iranian Tanker Company , which operates Iran’s fleet of state-owned oil tankers. Grand Target Heavy Equipment and Machinery Spare Parts Trading L.L.C, Recaz Star General Trading LLC, Meethale Raw Materials Trading Company LLC, Hemraj Trading L.L.C, Ewan Al Madeena General Trading LLC, OGA Global General Trading L.L.C, Dexterous Global DMCC, Khore Al Hilal Goods Wholesalers Trading LLC, Bogazici Gumrukleme Ithalat Ihracat Turizm Petrol Urunleri Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi, and Grandez Trading Limited are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. SHADOW BANKING FRONT COMPANIES Iranian exchange houses and rahbar companies operate through a multi-jurisdictional web of layered front and shell companies that enable them to remit and receive payments overseas on behalf of their Iranian customers. Iranian companies that participate in the global economy, in some way or fashion, engage with the Iranian shadow banking system to facilitate imports and exports. For example, Dubai-based Robust Trading LLC has facilitated payments for the sanctioned Iran-based copper mining giant National Iranian Copper Industries Company . Similarly, HMS Trading FZE , the Dubai-based oil export and commercial front company of Iranian Shahr Bank, has used Dubai-based Integral Petro Energy Trading LLC to facilitate millions of dollars’ worth of liquefied petroleum gas sales by Iranian petrochemical exporter Kharg Petrochemical Company Limited. Robust Trading LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13871 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services in support of, the National Iranian Copper Industries Company. Integral Petro Energy Trading LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, HMS Trading FZE. Other Dubai-based front companies include Royah Altahabia Trading L.L.C , Alam Al Sahra Building Materials Trading Co. L.L.C , Berkeley Trading LLC , and Nordic International Trading LLC , which have been counterparties to millions of dollars’ worth of transactions involving Iranian financial broker front companies operating within Iran’s rahbar system. Since at least 2022, Berkeley Trading L.L.C has facilitated millions of dollars’ worth of transactions for clients of Iran-based Amin Exchange. Royah Altahabia Trading L.L.C, Alam Al Sahra Building Materials Trading Co. L.L.C, Berkeley Trading LLC, and Nordic International Trading LLC are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Dubai-based Gespl International General Trading LLC has been used by the National Iranian Oil Company as part of its oil and petrochemicals sales mechanism and is actively involved in money laundering via Iran’s shadow banking mechanism. Gespl International General Trading LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petrochemical sector of the Iranian economy. Iran’s military organs also utilize the shadow banking system. Iranian Armed Forces General Staff-associated Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company (SEJ) and sanctioned shipping company Dragon Road Ltd utilized Dubai-based H N B Trading Co LLC to complete payment for the charter of the SERENE I (IMO 9197832); H N B Trading Co LLC received hundreds of thousands of dollars from a SEJ front company as part of this scheme. H N B Trading Co LLC is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company. IRAN CENTER FOR EXCHANGE Additionally, as part of today’s action, OFAC is taking action against the Iran-based Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold (Iran Center for Exchange), which plays an essential intermediary role within Iran’s system of international trade. The Iran Center for Exchange provides the financial plumbing to match exporters, who earn foreign currency from sales abroad, to importers, who need foreign currency to purchase goods, for tens of billions of dollars’ worth of trade every year. While Iran’s shadow banking system moves the funds generated by Iran’s international trade, the Iran Center for Exchange plays matchmaker and guides these funds to their ultimate destination inside Iran. The Central Bank of Iran also utilizes bonds issued by the Iran Center for Exchange to help facilitate international trade using Russian roubles and Chinese yuan without reliance on the U.S. dollar. The Iran Center for Exchange is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s OFAC action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.   OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions, unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades or conspires to violate U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. Financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons, including the persons designated today.  This includes, in addition to blocking prohibitions, that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List, when consistent with relevant statutes and other authorities.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is to bring about a positive change in behavior.  What constitutes a sufficient change in circumstance will vary based on context, including the status of the broader geopolitical circumstances affecting the national security and foreign policy interests implicated by the declared national emergency.  In the case of sanctions related to Iran, OFAC is employing all available statutory, regulatory, and policy tools to resolve the persistent national emergencies posed by Iran, which has not changed its behavior to align with U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives.  OFAC sanctions determinations, including removal determinations, are made consistent with Administration foreign policy and national security policies and priorities.  For more information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on How to Request Removal from an OFAC List. title: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Corrupt Regime Insiders Exploiting Iran’s Oil Sector for Personal Gain
body: November 20, 2026 WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury is targeting key “oil trustees” the Iranian regime relies on to facilitate the sale of oil abroad. With no oil on the water outside of the U.S. military blockade and no oil loaded onto vessels since the start of Operation Economic Outcast, the regime is attempting to recoup billions of dollars from its oil trustees.  In many cases, these corrupt trustees have kept the oil revenue for personal gain. “Iran’s tyrannical regime never fails to put its own interests before those of its own citizens, even as ordinary Iranians face shortages of bread and fuel,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “The regime has exhausted its seaborne oil supply, and it may never see the revenue from the oil it has already sold. The ship is sinking.” The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy, and E.O. 13224, as amended, a counterterrorism authority. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026, dubbed Economic D-Day , Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime.  Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror.  Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast has significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran.  Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. Operation Economic Outcast has also expanded sanctions exposure for non-U.S. persons who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . UNTRUSTWORTHY TRUSTEES Mohammad Javad Bavand (Bavand) and Majid Taj (Taj), the brother of the Iranian Football Federation’s president, operate as part of a network of regime insiders tasked with obtaining desperately needed cash by selling from Iran’s dwindling oil reserves.  Bavand, a former IRGC intelligence officer, has spearheaded this effort, entrusting a group of personal contacts, including Taj, to recoup Iran’s oil funds located in third countries.  The Iranian regime continues to entrust Bavand and Taj’s network with facilitating Iran’s oil sales, despite members owing billions of dollars to the regime from previous sales.  Bavand has worked with a variety of illicit oil trading actors, including the IRGC and Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company (SEJ), a U.S.-designated front company tasked with selling oil for the Iranian Armed Forces General Staff. Mohammad Javad Bavand and Majid Taj are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. REGIME FACILITATORS Mohammadhossein Servati (Servati), the son of IRGC Brigadier General Mohsen Servati, has held executive positions at companies operated by SEJ, including SEJ front company Xin Rui Jin Trad Co., Limited , and Sepehr Energy Hamta Pars , a subsidiary of SEJ.  Xin Rui Jin Trad Co., Limited brokered and received shipments of Iranian oil on behalf of SEJ for delivery to Chinese teapot refineries. Mohammadhossein Servati is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company. Mojtaba Arabnejad (Mojtaba) is the son of the designated Iranian businessman and CEO of Iran’s Mahan Air , Hamid Arabnejad .  Using his familial ties and special connections with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF), Mojtaba has been involved in purchasing aircraft parts for Mahan Air and procuring weapons for the Iranian military under the auspices of agricultural companies.  Like others designated today, Mojtaba has overseen oil sales for the Iranian regime, the proceeds from which have supported Mahan Air. Mojtaba Arabnejad is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Mahan Air. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions, unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades or conspires to violate U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the United States or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000.  Financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons, including the persons designated today.  This includes, in addition to blocking prohibitions, that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List, when consistent with relevant statutes and other authorities.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is to bring about a positive change in behavior.  What constitutes a sufficient change in circumstance will vary based on context, including the status of the broader geopolitical circumstances affecting the national security and foreign policy interests implicated by the declared national emergency.  In the case of sanctions related to Iran, OFAC is employing all available statutory, regulatory, and policy tools to resolve the persistent national emergencies posed by Iran, which has not changed its behavior to align with U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives.  OFAC sanctions determinations, including removal determinations, are made consistent with Administration foreign policy and national security policies and priorities.  For more information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on How to Request Removal from an OFAC List. title: Treasury Sanctions Major Drug Trafficking Organizations Supporting Terrorist Cartels
body: November 19, 2026 Coordinated Action with International Partners Targets a Cartel-Linked Outlaw Motorcycle Gang and Canadian-Based Mafia Leaders and Facilitators WASHINGTON —Today, the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two international drug trafficking organizations: the Australia-headquartered Comanchero Outlaw Motorcycle Gang ( Comancheros ) and the Italy-based ‘Ndrangheta , a mafia-type criminal syndicate.  By providing essential logistical and operational support, the Comancheros and ‘Ndrangheta help terrorist cartels expand their international reach and sustain global narcotrafficking networks. “Cartels do not operate in isolation. They rely on other criminal organizations like the Comancheros and ‘Ndrangheta to move drugs, launder illicit proceeds, and ultimately poison Americans with narcotics,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “Treasury will continue to expose and disrupt narcoterrorism networks to Keep America Safe.” The Comancheros and the ‘Ndrangheta operate sophisticated transnational criminal networks that facilitate large-scale drug trafficking and money laundering. The ‘Ndrangheta controls a significant share of the European cocaine trade, while the Comancheros have helped open access to some of the world's most lucrative illicit drug markets. In keeping with President Trump’s pledge to eliminate cartels, OFAC has prioritized targeting these and other criminal groups that threaten the welfare of Americans. Treasury has coordinated closely with the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF), taking nearly 40 actions against over 500 individuals and entities since the beginning of 2025.  OFAC uses a network-based approach to simultaneously disrupt as many different facets of the cartels as possible, from their leadership and key organizational nodes to facilitators and enablers, such as corrupt officials, complicit family members, and ostensibly legitimate front persons. Today’s action reflects a unified, whole-of-government effort to ensure operational coordination and maximize impact against transnational criminal networks.  OFAC conducted its investigation in parallel with the HSTF, with support from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Drug Enforcement Administration, and Homeland Security Investigations.  OFAC continues to work closely with the HSTF to disrupt the flow of illicit drugs and dismantle the networks, facilitators, and financial infrastructure that enable their production and distribution. Additionally, OFAC worked closely with valued international partners, including the Australian Federal Police, New Zealand Police, Italy’s Guardia di Finanza, and Canada’s Royal Canadian Mounted Police and York Regional Police, whose cooperation was instrumental in supporting today’s action. The action was taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 14059, which targets the proliferation of illicit drugs and their means of production. COMANCHERO OUTLAW MOTORCYCLE GANG Today, OFAC designated the Comancheros , also known as the Comanchero Motorcycle Club or simply Comanchero MC , an Australian drug trafficking organization with an international footprint in Asia, Europe, and North America.  Developing strategic partnerships with U.S. sanctioned cartels, including the Sinaloa Cartel, CJNG, Clan del Golfo, and Los Choneros, the Comancheros have facilitated multi-hundred-kilogram shipments of cocaine from South America to the United States, Australia, and Europe.  The Comancheros have also been involved in other criminal activity around the world, including assassinations, arms trafficking, and money laundering. Because Australia and New Zealand are some of the world’s most lucrative illicit drug markets, Mexican cartels are increasingly targeting these markets to capitalize on the significantly higher margins and growing demand.  Due to the geographic distance from the major cocaine producing regions in the Western Hemisphere, cartels can charge substantial premiums compared to drugs sold in the United States.  The Sinaloa Cartel has been known to send “sleeper cells” to Australia to facilitate local drug distribution and establish contacts with the Comancheros and other outlaw motorcycle gangs who assist with the logistics of drug trafficking. The Comancheros are being designated under E.O. 14059 for having engaged in, or having attempted to engage in, activities or transactions that have materially contributed to, or pose a significant risk of materially contributing to, the international proliferation of illicit drugs or their means of production. COMANCHERO COMMAND AND CONTROL Alexandre Varela Villar , better known as Alex Vare ( Vare ), is the Spain-based World Commander of the Comancheros. Allan John Norman Meehan , better known as Allan Meehan ( Meehan ), is the Australia-based World President of the Comancheros. Pasilika Naufahu ( Pasilika ) is the national president of the New Zealand chapter of the Comancheros.  Before being deported to New Zealand in 2016, Pasilika was the sergeant-at-arms of the Comancheros in Australia.  Pasilika was arrested and sentenced to 10 years in prison in February 2021 for various charges related to his position in the Comancheros.  In close coordination with his brother and senior Comancheros member, Vetekina Naufahu ( Vetekina ), Pasilika has facilitated multi-hundred-kilogram importations of drugs into New Zealand and has established connections to the Sinaloa Cartel. Marco Francis Coffen ( Coffen ) is an associate of the Comancheros and has been involved in supplying multiple Australian criminal organizations, including the Comancheros, with encrypted communication platforms to drug traffickers and shielding them from police phone taps. Vare and Meehan are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for being or having been leaders or officials of the Comancheros. Pasilika and Vetekina are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, the Comancheros. Coffen is being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having provided, or attempted to provide, financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services in support of, the Comancheros. OMERTÀ – THE ‘NDRANGHETA The ‘Ndrangheta , an international drug trafficking organization and mafia-type criminal syndicate, operates in over 80 countries and continues to grow.  The ‘Ndrangheta’s adherence to omertà , a code of silence, and its reliance on deeply rooted familial bloodlines have enabled the organization to maintain secrecy, foster loyalty, resist infiltration, and expand its criminal influence across generations and international borders.  While the ‘Ndrangheta was founded in Calabria, Italy, the organization has expanded across Europe, the Western Hemisphere, and Australia.  As one of the largest criminal organizations in the world, the ‘Ndrangheta’s primary business comes from drug trafficking, with some estimates stating that almost 80 percent of the European cocaine trade is controlled by the ‘Ndrangheta.  While primarily focused on the cocaine trade, Italian officials have stated that the ‘Ndrangheta have started expanding into the illicit fentanyl market. The ’Ndrangheta frequently partner with Mexican and South American drug trafficking organizations and FTOs, including the Sinaloa Cartel, CJNG, and Clan del Golfo.  In the past, the ‘Ndrangheta has also partnered with other Mexican drug trafficking organizations and FTOs, including Los Zetas (now known as Cartel del Noreste) and the Gulf Cartel. The ‘Ndrangheta was previously designated on May 30, 2008 , pursuant to the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act (Kingpin Act).  Today, the ‘Ndrangheta is being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having engaged in, or having attempted to engage in, activities or transactions that have materially contributed to, or pose a significant risk of materially contributing to, the international proliferation of illicit drugs or their means of production. ‘NDRANGHETISTI NORTH OF THE BORDER Locali (singular: locale ) are the primary territorial organizational unit of the ‘Ndrangheta, comprising members known as ‘ ndranghetisti , that oversee and coordinate criminal activities within a specific geographical region.  The ‘Ndrangheta locale that operates in the Greater Toronto Area in Canada has strengthened in recent years, becoming so powerful that they dictate events in Italy from across the ocean.  In Canada, the ‘Ndrangheta is involved in drug trafficking, money laundering, murder, and other crimes.  This faction of the ‘Ndrangheta uses the U.S. and Canadian financial systems to launder illicit proceeds. Today, OFAC designated Italian-born Angelo Figliomeni (also known as “Don Angelino”), the leader of the Toronto faction of the ‘Ndrangheta.  A member of the Figliomeni ‘ndrina (family), Angelo Figliomeni fled to Canada in the early 2000’s to escape a 20-year sentence for weapons charges in Italy.  Angelo’s power extends beyond Canada, stretching back to Italy.  He has engaged in money laundering and other criminal activities on behalf of the ‘Ndrangheta. Another member of the Figliomeni ‘ndrina is Italian-born Cosimo Figliomeni (sometimes known as “Cosimino”), who is a top leader of the ‘Ndrangheta faction in Toronto and has been the subject of criminal proceedings in Italy in connection to his role within the ‘Ndrangheta organization. OFAC also designated two members of the Commisso ‘ndrina who are long time Italian-born leaders of the ‘Ndrangheta in Toronto. Francesco Commisso , also known as “U Scelto,” has faced allegations in Italy of being part of a Toronto oversight body that was tasked, among other duties, with imposing disciplinary sanctions on members. Rocco Remo Commisso (also known as Remo Commisso ) is a Canada-based leader of the ‘Ndrangheta and leads narcotics trafficking networks within the United States, including in the state of New York.  Remo Commisso was convicted in Canada in 1981 for conspiracy to commit murder and again in 1984 for his involvement in a bombing that killed one person.  Remo Commisso is involved in narcotics trafficking in the United States for the ‘Ndrangheta, including in New York. Vincenzo DeMaria (also known as Jimmy DeMaria ) is one of Toronto’s top ‘Ndrangheta bosses and has been active in the Toronto organized crime scene for decades.  DeMaria shot and killed a man in 1981 over a $2,000 drug debt and was convicted of second-degree murder in 1982.  He has since been released from prison and holds significant power in the ‘Ndrangheta. Cosimo Figliomeni, Francesco Commisso, Remo Commisso, and Jimmy DeMaria make up the Camera di Controllo of Toronto, a collegial body of the ‘Ndrangheta that decides on important questions concerning the organization and settles disputes, even outside of Toronto.  The Toronto ‘Ndrangheta is tightly connected throughout the world and has close relationships with members back in Calabria. Luigi Vescio Sr. (also known as “The Undertaker” or “Lui Vescio”) is a Canadian-born ‘Ndrangheta senior member and associate of Angelo Figliomeni and Jimmy DeMaria. Angelo Figliomeni, Cosimo Figliomeni, Francesco Commisso, Remo Commisso, and Luigi Vescio Sr. were all charged in the Italian Court of Reggio Calabria for mafia-type association related to their leadership, membership, and promotion of the ‘Ndrangheta in 2019. Angelo Figliomeni, Cosimo Figliomeni, Francesco Commisso, Remo Commisso, Jimmy DeMaria, and Luigi Vescio Sr. are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, ‘Ndrangheta. FAMILY-OWNED, MAFIA-CONNECTED – VESCIO FUNERAL HOMES OFAC is also designating the corporate network of Vescio Sr., including his network of funeral homes in Ontario.  These funeral homes include the Fratelli Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Woodbridge, Ontario, Vescio Funeral Homes Ltd. in Toronto and Vescio Funeral Home (Maple) Inc. in Maple, Ontario.  Vescio Sr. also controls a Toronto-based luxury limousine rental business, Phantom Limousine Services Inc. Vescio Sr. serves as the president of each of these companies. OFAC is also designating Luigi Vescio Sr.’s wife, Rose Vescio , and his two children, Luigi Vescio Jr. and Laura Vescio , for their roles in owning and operating the Vescio Funeral Homes on behalf of Luigi Vescio Sr. Rose Vescio, Luigi Vescio Jr., and Laura Vescio are being designated pursuant to E.O. 14059 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Luigi Vescio Sr. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  Unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  In addition, financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities involving designated or otherwise blocked persons.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List), but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior.  For information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on Filing a Petition for Removal from an OFAC List . title: Treasury Targets Cyber Scam Operators and Armed Group Facilitators in Southeast Asia
body: November 19, 2026 WASHINGTON —Today, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned three individuals involved in operating and facilitating cyber scam centers in Southeast Asia, as well as two affiliated companies.  The individuals designated today include operators of scam compounds that target Americans through virtual currency investment fraud and affiliates of armed groups that provide protection and support to scam-center networks in Southeast Asia. “Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted overseas scam compounds to protect Americans from fraud,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “We will continue to use all available tools to disrupt and dismantle the networks that enable scam compounds to operate.” These actions are being taken in furtherance of President Trump’s Executive Order (E.O.) 14390 of March 6, 2026, “Combating Cybercrime, Fraud, and Predatory Schemes Against American Citizens,” which orders the U.S. Government to unleash every available tool to stop foreign-backed criminal networks that exploit vulnerable Americans through cybercrime, cyber-enabled fraud, and extortion.  Today’s action further reflects OFAC’s coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s New York Field Office, Department of Justice’s Scam Center Strike Force, and the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Homeland Security Task Force and National Coordination Center.  OFAC is taking today’s actions pursuant to E.O. 13694, as amended by E.O. 13757, E.O. 14144, and E.O. 14306 (“E.O. 13694, as further amended”). ZHAO HUI: A SCAM CENTER OPERATOR Zhao Hui (Zhao) is a Cambodian national who leased a scam center owned by the OFAC-designated Prince Group TCO and paid protection fees to the OFAC-designated leader of the Prince Group TCO, Chen Zhi .  In addition, Zhao owned a scam compound in Cambodia independent of Prince Group TCO.  At this scam compound, Zhao was directly involved in scam operations and managed this scam compound’s leases.  This scam compound primarily targeted Americans and Europeans.  Such scam compounds conduct virtual currency investment scams.  Since Zhao has leased a scam compound and owned and operated an additional scam compound in Cambodia, he has materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of virtual cryptocurrency investment scams, an activity described in subsection 1(a)(ii) of E.O. 13694, as further amended. Zhao is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13694, as further amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, an activity described in subsection 1(a)(ii) of E.O. 13694, as further amended. Zhao is the chairman of the board of directors of Cambodia-based construction company Bei Fang Bo Lin Construction Decoration Co., Ltd . (Bei Fang Bo Lin) and management and consultancy company ZHZ Investment Consulting Co., Ltd. (ZHZ Investment). Bei Fang Bo Lin and ZHZ Investment are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13694, as further amended, for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Zhao Hui. THE DKBA’S FACILITATION OF SCAM COMPOUND ACTIVITY In recent years, armed groups in Burma have transformed a strip along the Thai-Burmese border into one of the world’s highest concentrations of scam centers.  The Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) is an ethnic armed group previously designated by OFAC for supporting cyber scam centers in Burma that target Americans using fraudulent investment schemes.  DKBA actors not only provide security for scam compounds and permit their continued operation, but also actively participate in violence against victims of human trafficking trapped inside the compounds. Since December 2025, General Saw Shwe Wah has been the commander-in-chief of the DKBA, replacing General Saw Steel , who OFAC designated in November 2025 pursuant to E.O. 13694, as further amended. Colonel Saw A One is the DKBA commander who oversees security in the Three Pagodas Pass in Karen State near the Thai border.  The region has seen expansion of new buildings intended for telecom scam operations, with many scam actors entering the area with the assistance of the DKBA, which also protects them.  Saw A One reportedly owns a plantation where scam operations occur and has contracted for scam operations. Saw Shwe Wah and Saw A One are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13694, as further amended, for being or having been leaders, officials, senior executive officers, or members of the board of directors of the DKBA, a person whose property and interests in property are blocked pursuant to E.O. 13694, as further amended. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  Unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S.  persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated or otherwise blocked persons.
